And if the US isn't going to do that, how is it going to maintain an an economy capable of supporting the vast military-industrial complex that it needs to be global policeman. >> That was Rabobank geostrategist Michael [music] Every. I'm Eric Townsend, and this is Macro Voices, the free weekly podcast targeting professional finance and sophisticated private investors. Episode 557 was produced on November 5th, 2026. This week's topic has to be the US midterm elections and their impacts on markets. And who better to cover that topic than Rabobank's Michael Every? We'll discuss the blue tsunami in the midterms, market implications of the data center moratoria, and how President Trump's likely growing conflicts with Congress will affect both the Iran and the Ukraine conflicts. >> And I'm Patrick Ceresna. Let's dive straight into this interview. >> Joining me now is Rabobank's global strategist Michael Every. Michael, it's great to have you back. Obviously, US elections and their consequences for financial markets are the only plausible topic for this week's show. Why don't we just dive in from the top? What's your take in terms of I think it's pretty darn clear that the Democrats took both houses of Congress, but let's go to the next level. What should we see that maybe not everyone is seeing? >> Everyone is rightly talking about what a political shock this is within the US system. What perhaps not everyone fully grasps in all of its complexities is what a shock it is for the world in a geopolitical context because what happens in America doesn't stay in America. And if things are going to be changing in America, they're going to change for everyone else, too. >> Okay. Let's talk about the things that are going change for everyone else. Obviously the the big question, I think what seems to me like the biggest question, is the Democrats have already vowed to stop the Iran war. Uh of course congressional approval is theoretically required for wars but doesn't seem to always in practice be required. Is that going to change? Are the Democrats going to push that? And particularly, what levers do they have? Is is there a funding cutoff? You know, if Democrats say you can't have a war without our approval because we've got the Congress and the president says, well I'm the president, I'm going to do what I want. What can they do to stop him? >> On that long constitutional grass remains to be seen. The power of the purse is significant. But I think the perhaps more pertinent point is it's difficult enough to win a war anyway, particularly in the Middle East and we can see that very clearly at the moment. It's enormously harder when you're fighting a political war at home and you don't even have the backing of Congress, let alone of the public. So that's only going to make it harder for the US to continue to act longer term, at least after January when we get the new Congress sitting and that's an important caveat there. But that itself has enormous ramifications because if this is something that's going to be the norm, just not for this war but more generally that the US is now constrained on foreign policy by a Congress that doesn't want the kind of adventures that have been quite normal up until recently, it means that the US is a greatly constrained geopolitical actor, were that to be true. >> If the US becomes greatly constrained, it seems that Israel no longer has a partner in this war. Does that end the war? Does it leave Israel in Iran fighting a different war that the US steps out of? How does that evolve? >> Well again, remains to be seen. It's a very fluid situation. But it can, on one level if you look at a a rough spectrum of outcomes, it can see the ultimate taco, which you know I've always thrown could be the whole enchilada of the US saying well we're done with the Middle East because if they're done here they're done in the Middle East full stop which obviously changes the global energy complex obviously changes the great game that's being played between the US China and others in terms of you know control of regions and resources and supply chains and really tells the region that you're on your own now and power abhors a vacuum. So in other words you either end up with a region which is pretty much being bossed by America's geostrategic opponents which obviously comes at a cost from America Inc and Americans back home whether they recognize the reality of America Inc or not or it's a region which is being destabilized by rival powers trying to fill that power vacuum that used to be held by the US. In neither case at least short term does that make an argument for lower energy prices? >> It seems to me at the risk of bringing up the awkward topic that Israel is a nuclear state if they no longer have the support of the United States in a conventional war it sounds to me like there is a risk of a a nuclear escalation because without the assistance of the United States they can't win the war any other way. Is that a risk? >> One doesn't rule anything in or out, but I have to say I still think that's an extremely fat tail risk and nothing more than that. And you know, there's a there's a good reason for that. First of all, to to cross that red line, particularly as a small country rather than a great power, would have enormous enormous implications for Israel. So that would really be a last moment life or death option. And secondly, the heuristic is such the back in the Yom Kippur war of 1973, which in the early stages saw genuine fears within Israel that it was going to lose and be wiped off the map. Even at that stage, Prime Minister Golda Meir didn't reach for the red button. So I'm not saying it's impossible. I'm not saying that the increasingly common possibility of brandishing it about as a threat couldn't happen, but it's certainly not something that I think we need to lose too much sleep over, at least not for the moment. >> Is Israel believed to have tactical nuclear weapons, the equivalent of dial a yield where they can use a limited nuclear strike or is it kind of an all or nothing thing for them? >> I don't believe they have tactical nuclear weapons, and I still think that would open the same can of worms for them as a smaller economy, particularly because just to show how muddy these waters get, if we are going to see an aggressive decoupling of the Israeli and American military going forward, which by the way is not the face of legislation currently still working its way through the old Congress, which would actually link them up at the R&D level. And India would not be too thrilled with Israel starting to brandish nuclear weapons. So I can think it'd be easily boxed in before it even began to think about doing something like that. >> Let's come back to much more realistic and likely outcomes, including one that I think is pretty darn certain at this point, which is data centers are going to be paused in a bunch of states. Some people are actually using the phrase regime change in Texas to describe the uh what's just happened there. So, why don't we do a quick summary of that and what are the implications of these data center pauses that have been announced already by Democrats as obviously a remedy or a mitigation for high electric bills? >> Sure. So, there are a lot of kind of conflated points that come into this, which is first of all, there's still a wall of money being thrown at that sector. And at the same time, the US at the highest level for now, and I would imagine after they've been after they've been briefed, even the new Democratic Congress are going to be told that certain individuals still see this as a national security issue rather than just an economic issue. And as such, you know, China can't be allowed to get ahead in this Sputnik style or Manhattan Project style race. So, that dynamic may still play out in the background. And there's widespread recognition that this needs to be done.
